clinicalPearls: A fibrocellular membrane proliferating on the inner surface of the retina at the macula, common in older adults and often bilateral though usually asymmetric
Most cases are idiopathic and related to posterior vitreous detachment; secondary membranes follow retinal tears or detachment, vascular occlusion, uveitis, trauma or intraocular surgery
Symptoms depend on severity and range from none, through a subtle cellophane sheen, to metamorphopsia, reduced acuity and micropsia as contraction increases
Fundus examination shows glistening or wrinkled inner retina with distorted, straightened or dragged retinal vessels
Optical coherence tomography is the key investigation, demonstrating the membrane, retinal thickening, loss of the foveal pit and, in advanced cases, a lamellar or pseudohole
The Amsler grid is a simple bedside and home tool for detecting and monitoring distortion
Many mild membranes remain stable and warrant observation, with intervention reserved for troublesome distortion or declining vision
Management of visually significant disease is surgical, with pars plana vitrectomy and membrane peel, often including internal limiting membrane peel
reference.pathophysiology: An epiretinal membrane forms when glial cells, retinal pigment epithelial cells and other cell types migrate onto and proliferate along the inner retinal surface, laying down a contractile fibrocellular sheet. In idiopathic cases this is typically triggered by a posterior vitreous detachment that leaves residual cortical vitreous and breaks in the internal limiting membrane, allowing cells to gain access to the retinal surface. Contraction of the membrane wrinkles the underlying retina, distorts the foveal architecture and displaces retinal vessels, producing metamorphopsia and reduced acuity. Persistent traction can cause macular oedema and, uncommonly, a lamellar or full-thickness macular hole.
additionalDifferentials: Choroidal neovascular membrane in age-related macular degeneration
additionalInvestigations: Optical coherence tomography to characterise the membrane, foveal contour and retinal thickness
Amsler grid testing to quantify and monitor metamorphopsia
Best-corrected visual acuity measurement to track functional change
Fundus examination and imaging to detect vessel distortion and any macular hole
Fluorescein angiography where secondary vascular pathology or leakage is suspected
Assessment for underlying causes such as prior retinal tears, vascular occlusion or uveitis in secondary cases
redFlags: Rapidly worsening distortion or acuity suggesting progressive traction
Development of a lamellar or full-thickness macular hole
Features of an underlying secondary cause such as retinal vascular occlusion or a retinal tear
New symptoms suggesting associated retinal detachment
reference.prognosis: Many idiopathic membranes remain stable with good vision; when surgery is performed for visually significant disease, distortion and acuity usually improve, though recovery is gradual and often incomplete, and some residual metamorphopsia may persist.
pitfalls: Attributing reduced vision to a mild membrane while missing a coexisting cause such as macular oedema or neovascular disease
Overlooking a secondary membrane and failing to identify and treat the underlying pathology
Recommending surgery for a stable, minimally symptomatic membrane
Missing an evolving macular hole beneath the membrane on OCT
Setting unrealistic expectations about the speed and completeness of visual recovery after peeling
